claims.text: Rapid thermal processing can kinetically trap noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles in a metastable single-phase solid-solution state.
Slower cooling increases atomic diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Increased diffusion during slower cooling enables thermodynamically driven phase separation and elemental segregation.
The initial nanoparticles contain more than five elements.
Rapid-heating and rapid-cooling conditions yield a metastable single-phase solid solution in the initial state.
Cooling rate controls the extent of diffusion-enabled compositional reordering.
Rapid cooling leaves insufficient atomic mobility for equilibrium compositional reordering.
The insufficient mobility under rapid cooling kinetically traps the high-entropy single-phase state.
Slowing the cooling rate gives atoms additional time to diffuse.
Thermodynamically favorable interactions activated by the additional diffusion drive phase separation and elemental segregation.
Relative to rapid cooling, slower cooling will produce more observable phase separation.
Relative to rapid cooling, slower cooling will increase elemental segregation.
Relative to rapid cooling, slower cooling will alter particle morphology as a result of enhanced atomic diffusion.
The proposed relationship applies when composition is fixed, rapid heating is retained, and cooling rate can be controlled.
Extreme atomic-size or mixing-enthalpy disparities may dominate over diffusion kinetics and limit applicability of the hypothesis.
The cooling-rate threshold for transition from a single phase to phase-separated structures depends on the diffusion characteristics of the constituent elements.
